question: What area counts as Masjid al-Aqsa, and is the Dome of the Rock part of it?
answer:
Now, another point that is relevant is what exactly constitutes Masjid al-Aqsa. I forgot to show you a picture, but you can look up any picture on the internet and you can find the map of the entire area.

There's a lot of misunderstanding when it comes to defining the actual, precise location of Masjid al-Aqsa, because there is a complex in Jerusalem that is massive. There's over 30 acres of land, a large piece of land. To walk the entire perimeter will take you maybe 10 minutes, 20 minutes or so; actually more than this. And it is shared by multiple faith traditions. The Muslims have the largest space over there, and then there is the Wailing Wall on another side of it, where the Jewish people go to say their prayers as well. It's a massive complex.

And within the complex you have iconic structures. The most iconic structure is the famous Dome of the Rock. This is the dome that is golden and turquoise blue in color. And it was built by 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan in the first century of the Hijrah, around 60 years after the Hijrah of the Prophet ﷺ, 70 years after the Hijrah of the Prophet ﷺ. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan built this magnificent structure that was considered to be the most beautiful masjid of its time, and he brought the greatest architects to build it. And he built it on top of a mini hill or a small mountain that used to be the center of the complex. So there was a mountain (it's still there, obviously), and he built the dome on top of this rock; that's why it's called the Dome of the Rock.

And this rock is alleged to be (alleged; it's not authentic, but these are stories that are told) the place where our Prophet ﷺ went up in al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj; he went up to the heavens from the rock. Now, this is just a tale that is told; it is not found in the actual books of the seerah. We do not know where our Prophet ﷺ stood when he began the ascent. Maybe he stood on the rock, maybe he didn't; we don't know. Nonetheless, the legends later on love to make up all of the details and fill in the gaps. And so the common folklore and the legends of the people to this day is that the rock was where he was taken up to the heavens from. In reality, the rock is not considered to be any extra holy or not. The whole region is holy; it's not just that rock.

Now, there's a lot of talk (and I don't want to go into too much detail) that there are accusations, let us say, that 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan built this magnificent Dome of the Rock in order to bring people to visit Masjid al-Aqsa. And so he wanted to build a structure, basically we would say, for tourism and for a political goal as well, because at that time frame Mecca and Medina were not in his control; they were under the control of 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr. Now, I don't want to go into a lot of detail, but to be very simple about this: we don't care what his intentions were. The land is holy, really. It doesn't matter if he hired the best architects because he wanted tourism, because he wanted people to come, because he wanted to make himself more prestigious and whatnot. That is between him and Allah 'azza wa jall. We don't care what his intentions were. At the end of the day, it is a blessed land and area, and he did build a magnificent structure, and we can marvel at the architecture. But we should be aware that the Dome of the Rock is not exclusively Masjid al-Aqsa.

A lot of people, when they think of Masjid al-Aqsa, think of the Dome of the Rock. We say: nothing wrong, you can think of the Dome of the Rock, but realize the Dome of the Rock is in the center, and it is much, much larger than this. Now, other people get very irritated, and they say, "How dare you show the Dome of the Rock with the title Masjid al-Aqsa? This is wrong." And they say Masjid al-Aqsa is the masjid that is in front of the dome, and not the dome. So they say it is wrong to show the picture of the Dome of the Rock and call it Masjid al-Aqsa. And we say to this: you are incorrect to say that this is incorrect, because the dome is a part of Masjid al-Aqsa, and the masjid you're referring to is also a part of Masjid al-Aqsa. So there's nothing wrong with showing a picture of the Dome of the Rock, but we educate the people that the Dome of the Rock is a part of the masjid.

In fact, Ibn Taymiyyah says that Masjid al-Aqsa is the term or the title given to the entire complex that Sulayman 'alayhi al-salam built. It's not just one small spot; it is a massive area. And he said some people later on restricted Masjid al-Aqsa to be the mosque at the front of the complex, and it is not to be restricted. In other words, it is a mistake of all sides to consider Masjid al-Aqsa to be one part of the complex.

On the contrary, even the complex as it currently stands is an estimation. We are estimating roughly. Neither we nor the Jewish people know exactly where the foundations of the temple were. And that is because the temple of Sulayman was built thousands of years ago, and it was destroyed completely, multiple times. Now, I know if you go to Aqsa, some of the guys will point to some of the rocks and stones and say, "This is the original temple of Sulayman." And the fact of the matter, once again, is that this is folklore, this is legend. In all likelihood, what they are showing you is Roman reconstructions, from the time of the Romans, I should say.

And that is King Herod, H-E-R-O-D. King Herod was actually a Jewish king, believe it or not. It's a very interesting story: the Roman empire allowed him to be a mini king of the city of Jerusalem. And so he wanted to rebuild the temple of Sulayman, in the time of Jesus Christ. This is not Sulayman; no, this is very late. So this is a building that is Roman in nature; it was built by Roman architects, and its style is Roman. But King Herod built it, and he wanted to estimate. And so he guessed that this would be the exact location. We know, of course, the generic location, the center of Jerusalem, but the exact demarcation we do not know. So the king built this temple, and that too was destroyed 40 years after Jesus Christ.

So King Herod rebuilt the temple before the coming of Jesus. When Maryam 'alayha al-salam was growing up, that was when King Herod built the temple. Jesus saw the temple of Herod. He saw that temple; he interacted with that temple. Then after Jesus Christ, that temple was completely destroyed. When our Prophet ﷺ visited it, by the way, technically the city did not have any temple whatsoever. They had converted it into a dump for the trash, because they did not respect the Jewish sanctity of that region.

Nonetheless, the point is that we do not know exactly the demarcations of the temple. So as a guesstimate, as an estimation, the area that we now call the complex is what has been considered to be the original. However, in all likelihood it is slightly larger than this, and maybe even to the entire city the blessings apply. So the point being, we should not be so technical that when we step outside of that complex, the blessings finish. On the contrary, that entire region, and frankly the entire city of Jerusalem, and especially the old city of Jerusalem, all of it can be considered to be sacred and holy. **But for us, what we call the complex, and even beyond the complex, can constitute Masjid al-Aqsa.** So in that entire area, if we were to pray two raka'ah, or do dhikr or Qur'an or charity or whatnot, it is extra rewarded in that entire complex.
